newsitem.title: GERMANY: Thyssen telecoms business set to grow.
newsitem.headline: Thyssen telecoms business set to grow.

text.p: Thyssen Telecom AG, the telecommunications unit of German steel group Thyssen AG, said on Tuesday turnover nearly tripled in the 1995/96 business year and start-up losses were in line with expectations.

Finance chief Stefan Baustert told reporters in Duesseldorf that sales in the business year that ended on September 30 rose to 184.5 million marks ($118 million) from 66.3 million marks the year before.

"Business results for the Telecom group developed in line with the planned start-up losses," he said. "Adjusted for new acquisitions and start-ups, expansion reached a factor of 2.6 -- that is stable growth."
Two of the companies' seven subsidiaries ended the year with a profit, he said, but declined to elaborate.

Financial investments totalled 335 million marks -- most of which for a 1.75 percent stake in the E-Plus mobile phone company, boosting Thyssen's E-Plus stake to 30.125 percent. Another 43 million marks were invested in material assets.
Other E-Plus investors include Veba AG, 30.125 percent, BellSouth, 22.507 percent, and Vodafone, 17.243 percent.
Total financing so far for E-Plus from all investors combined totals 4.2 billion marks.

Thyssen Telecom acquisitions and start-ups in 1995/96 included the IS Internet Services firm, call centre operator Dialok, online services firm Ontel and the formation of a Swiss subsidiary of the corporate network unit PlusNet AG.
In its first two years of operation Thyssen Telecom has invested around 650 million marks, including outlay for E-Plus.
Baustert said the company slashed planned investment for the next five years to around 700 million marks from earlier forecasts of up to four billion marks.
"The reason for this reduced outlay is a revision of strategy in public telephony which was forced upon us by the extremely slow liberalisation of this market," he said.
Commenting on E-Plus, Baustert said the mobile phone group would have 550,000 subscribers by the end of 1996 and achieve network penetration of 90 percent of the population.

"E-Plus will achieve break even as planned in 1998," said Hans-Erich Forster, Thyssen Telecom chairman. "It is clear that the mobile phone market will continue its dynamic development with annual growth rates of at least 15 percent."
Over the next few years E-Plus could increasing come out of the corner as Germany's junior cellular network, compared to the larger D1 and D2 networks owned by Deutsche Telekom and Mannesmann.

One of the main drawbacks facing E-Plus has been the lack of compatible partner networks. E-Plus operates according to the DCS 1800 digital cellular standard, which is not compatible with the GSM standard of the other two networks.
The GSM standard is also more common in the rest of Europe, which has meant until now that when an E-Plus customer left Germany, it was not possible in most places to make calls.

But that is changing. More DCS 1800 licences are being awarded across Europe and mobile phone makers are set to introduce so-called dual-mode phones that can switch between GSM and DCS 1800 frequencies.
"These phones will eliminate the last remaining disadvantage compared to the D-networks," Baustert said.

Hans-Peter Kohlhammer, Thyssen Telecom managing director, said the company's Internet provision business was growing 30 percent a month. Its Internet Service company has 50,000 residential customers and 230,000 business customers. ($ = 1.563 German Marks)
